aniki-bobo-1942.gazette: Denied a studio, Oliveira moved the production onto the streets of Porto and shot the city as it stood: riverfront stairs, shopfronts, the Douro traffic passing behind the boys. The constraint became the method — real light, real streets, children who lived there. Italy arrived at the same contract a year later and eventually gave it a name.

ossessione-1943.gazette: Wartime Italian screens ran to drawing rooms and white telephones. Visconti went to the Po valley instead and shot roadside inns, flat farmland, and people with nothing, undressed. The Fascist censors moved against the film; the method outlived them and came back after the war under the name neorealism.

bicycle-thieves-1948.gazette: The lead was a factory worker and the boy was found on the street. American money was available on the condition that a Hollywood star play the father; De Sica kept the worker and shot in a Rome where a bicycle was the difference between a wage and none. The picture went out to a country that recognized its own pavement.
bicycle-thieves-1948.prism: That refusal is the whole film in miniature — a star would have made the loss survivable, because stars survive. Casting a man who actually needed the job is what turns the last scene into a verdict instead of a plot point.

los-olvidados-1950.gazette: Before shooting, Buñuel walked the tenement districts on the edge of Mexico City and cast children out of the neighborhoods he had been watching. Mexico took the picture as an insult and pulled it from cinemas within days of the opening. Cannes reversed the verdict the following year, and it came home a classic.

forbidden-games-1952.gazette: It opens on the 1940 exodus — a road south, families on foot, aircraft coming in low — and then hands itself over to two children in a farmhouse. Clément shot their games at their own pace, without the polish French cinema usually applied to child performers. What the war does offscreen, the children rehearse in a barn, burying animals and stealing crosses for the graves.

summer-with-monika-1953.gazette: The archipelago summer was the schedule and the subject both. Bergman worked with a small crew on available light — skin, water, weather, nothing hauled in to flatter anyone — and let the season end inside the film, returning the couple to a city apartment and a wage. Distributors abroad recut it and sold it as smut.
summer-with-monika-1953.prism: The swimming was never the transgression; the transgression is the second half, where summer ends and someone has to make rent. Sold as a bad-girl picture, it is really an account of what freedom costs when only one person keeps paying for it.

pather-panchali-1955.gazette: There was no studio and no reliable money. Ray shot on weekends over several years in a village outside Calcutta, stopping each time the funds ran out, with a cameraman who had never shot a film and a cast that had mostly never acted. The West Bengal government paid to finish it, and the finished thing went around the world.

aparajito-1956.gazette: For the second Apu film Ray took his camera onto the ghats at Benares and shot the pilgrims, the barbers, and the wrestlers as they were, then followed the boy back to a Bengal village and on to a Calcutta printing press. Bengali audiences preferred the first film; Venice gave this one its top prize. The method had not changed — location, ordinary faces, the ordinary duration of a childhood ending.

sweet-smell-of-success-1957.gazette: Broadway after dark, in real traffic outside real clubs: James Wong Howe shot the picture where the trade it depicts was still being conducted nightly. Planting items, trading girls for paragraphs, keeping a columnist fed — the press agent's work is rendered as an ordinary job with ordinary hours. Audiences who bought tickets for Lancaster and Curtis got a portrait of the men selling them their gossip, and stayed away.
sweet-smell-of-success-1957.prism: It failed commercially because it named the machine its own audience was plugged into, a column that could make or unmake a person by lunchtime. The city looks magnificent in Howe's night photography, which is the trick — the glamour is the product, and the deal always happens just outside the light.

cairo-station-1958.gazette: The terminal kept working while the picture was shot inside it: porters, luggage carts, the hawkers who slept on the platforms. Chahine cut real station footage into a drama about the men who lived off the trains, and played the lame news vendor himself. Egyptian audiences rejected it on release, and it sat for years before Europe called it a landmark.

the-world-of-apu-1959.gazette: Apu is in a rented room over the Calcutta rail line, behind on rent, with a novel nobody has bought. Ray staged the wedding in a river village reached by boat and kept the ceremony's actual rhythm rather than a compressed version of it. Both leads were new to film, and neither performance looks like acting.

rocco-and-his-brothers-1960.gazette: A night train out of Lucania, a basement flat in Milan: Visconti set the film in the years when the North was absorbing southern migrants by the trainload into its factories and cheap rooms. He shot the city those migrants actually got — the periphery, the boxing gyms, the fog off the water at the Idroscalo. The economic miracle appears only as something happening to other people.
rocco-and-his-brothers-1960.prism: The family doesn't fail to assimilate; it gets precisely what the boom was offering, which was piecework, a basement, and a way out through the ring. Milan's prosperity in those years ran on people it housed badly and never counted as its own.

the-naked-island-1960.gazette: No one in the film speaks. Shindo took a crew small enough to feed on site out to a bare island in the Seto Inland Sea and filmed one family hauling fresh water up the terraces by shoulder pole, trip after trip, season after season. The company behind it was near collapse; the grand prize at Moscow kept the doors open.

accattone-1961.gazette: Pasolini had been writing about the Roman borgate for years before he directed anything; for his first film he went back to the same outskirts and cast the people he had been writing about, Franco Citti among them. The pimps, the dust, the half-built blocks at the edge of the city are locations, not sets dressed to resemble them. Over that he laid Bach, the only thing in the film that did not come from the neighborhood.

aimless-bullet-1961.gazette: The city was already the set. Yu shot in the ruins and refugee shanties still standing in Seoul eight years after the armistice, so nothing had to be built and nothing had to be faked. Within months of release the new military government pulled the film from cinemas, and it stayed off Korean screens for years.
aimless-bullet-1961.prism: A film gets banned for showing rubble only when the rubble is still there and the state would rather it weren't. The realism contract cut both ways here: nothing had to be constructed, and nothing could be denied.
